name: Murle
confidence_why: Arensen 1982, the only first-hand Murle grammar read, puts stress and high tone on a long-vowel syllable and otherwise usually on the first syllable, and the older group-level survey by Tucker and Bryan 1966 names no stress position but likewise ties stress to vowel length, so nothing contradicts the record though it rests on a single self-hedged description.

catalog_quote: However, my findings show that on the word level, tone does not have lexical significance. In an isolated word, tone is closely connected with stress and lengthened vowels, and the three must be considered as one entity. When a word has a lengthened vowel, the high tone and stress also occur on the syllable with the lengthened vowel. If there is no lengthened vowel in a two-syllable word, then the stress and high tone are usually put on the first syllable.* /kádak/ 'to eat' /kadáak/ 'to die' Words of three or more syllables are more unpredictable, although again the stress and high tone usually go on the first syllable if there is no syllable with a lengthened vowel. /kíziwan/ 'buffalo' /motóoŋtoc/ 'tamarind tree' ... new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (qs-tier-2026-09-12) carries an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so there is no placement to agree with or contradict. Tucker & Bryan add: the group is tonal (three levels, lexical and grammatical tone) and stress is 'little known' with length as a possible correlate, and they name no stress position. This is compatible with the WALS 'No fixed stress' value noted in the earlier check for Murle (Goedemans & van der Hulst, from Arensen 1982) and with an empty placement. Statement is group-level; the example is Didinga, not Murle.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Didinga-Murle group as a whole (Didinga, Longarim, Murle) the book records three level tones plus rising and falling tone, with lexical and grammatical function, and says only that little is known about stress; a stressed syllable may sometimes carry vowel length or be followed by a lengthened consonant (the one example is Didinga). No placement rule is given for Murle or for the group.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only Murle-specific prosodic remark in the chapter is that 'Lyth, however, frequently doubles the vowels in his MURLE material', i.e. a spelling/length matter, not stress
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat DIDINGA, LONGARIM and MURLE together as 'The Didinga-Murle Group' (ch. 27, pp. 370-391); the sec. 2 Tone and Stress statement is group-level and its one example is Didinga. Murle sources named at the chapter head (p. 370): A. N. Tucker, MS. notes; Tucker, 'Notes on Murle ("Beir")', Afrika und Übersee 1952; R. E. Lyth, A Murle Grammar, cyclostyled, 1947. A 'Tone and Stress appear to be significant, both lexically and grammatically: eli Arrive!..' passage that the same query returns belongs to the KUNAMA chapter (Barka dialect context), not to Didinga-Murle.

readall_conflicts: Only one work was listed and opened, so there is no disagreement among the works read here. For context: the sibling check record for Didinga, read held by the project, not a work in this list) quotes Odden 1983: 151 as stating that Didinga has two tones (H, L) and that, 'contrary to suggestions by Driberg or Tucker and Bryan, there is nothing which could be called stress' — a later Didinga-specific rejection of the stress remark, and two tones rather than Tucker & Bryan's three levels; that concerns Didinga, not Murle. The earlier check for Murle recorded WALS 14A 'No fixed stress' / 15A 'Unbounded' / 16A 'Long vowel' (Goedemans & van der Hulst, from Arensen 1982) and WALS 13A 'Simple tone system'; Tucker & Bryan's group-level 'little is known about stress.. vowel length' is compatible with those values but does not establish them.
